text:
I like the article. And I fully agree on the remark that (in my words) science is not (and in my opinion should never be) settled. Whenever we learn or experience something new, existing science might need to be adapted.
This also holds for general knowledge. The older I get the more the feeling grows that there is so much I do not know. LLMs on the other hand seem to act contrary, everything seems a hard fact in the way it is told. And I think/seem to see that a lot of people put a lot of trust in these ‘facts’.
So the best option for me remains: keep an open mind and think for myself. Not always easy though to not get caught in existing believes and previous experiences.

text:
You have to know quite a bit about LLMs to do a good job - as with other powerful tools. And it would help a lot if we had more transparent LLMs, whose learning set could be scrutinized.

Perhaps the two biggest issues with LLMs, other than their huge negative externalities, are opacity and the exceptional ease for using them badly.

text: Just about everything possible is happening with LLMs in science at the moment. Many people use them as tools to help them with their research, or just with writing their reports. Some check the output, others don't. There are plenty of scientific publications with hallucinated references, or telltale phrases such as "Certainly, here is the paragraph you asked for:". Publications completely written by LLMs (based on no human research work at all) remain very rare, but a few made it into some conference proceedings.

text:
Lots of things! I struggle to encapsulate it all, but I think there's a critical and creative and at times philosophical aspect to code, which loops back to poetry (or a poetic spirit) for me. It's always been interesting to me to draw parallels between code and poetry — they're both very particular forms of writing, except one evokes emotion and one invokes some action (and may evoke emotion, too). Adding on to that, in a time when people are increasingly content to let LLMs generate code, I find it really meaningful for myself to grapple with the craft of writing code. How can we understand it critically (syntax, style, context — see the field of critical code studies) but also see opportunities for creativity and imagination as focused on code and coding practices?

Not sure if I went too abstract there, but maybe short answer is that I really like writing code and have a strong emotional attachment to it, and that's the poetic tug for me. :slightly_smiling_face:
